quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

"Herm" is almost certainly an index truncation of "Hermann"; the underlying manifest's spelling cannot be verified without the original record. Identity of this passenger with tree subject I1 (Hermann Gaetjen, born ~1859) is uncertain: the stated birth year 1854 differs from the tree subject's approximate birth year by five years. This identity question must be resolved by corroborating evidence, not asserted from this index alone.

Birth year 1854 as stated in the index conflicts with the tree subject I1's approximate birth year of ~1859 — a five-year discrepancy that raises an identity question. Notably, the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry (src_001) records a Hermann Gatjen aged 21, implying birth ~1854, which is consistent with this index entry; the two may record the same individual. Whether that individual is the same as tree subject I1 requires independent corroboration. The birth year in a passenger index would typically derive from the passenger's self-reported age or a birth year column on the original manifest; neither can be verified without the original.

Prussia is a broad political designation covering a large territory, not a specific locality. It does not identify a German province, town, or parish of origin. The index records no departure port or ship name, so the original manifest — which may carry a more specific origin — cannot be located from this entry alone.

Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
I did not create a link for a_002. The baptism record's principal is a Patrick Flynn, but the record gives his birthplace as Trier, Rhine Province, Germany, and the tree attests Ireland (about 1845). That birthplace conflict is a core-identifier contradiction, so the match is Weak and gets no link, even though the same-person score is 0.85. The score cannot override a qualitative conflict.

What I checked:
- **a_002** is the name assertion ("Patrick Flynn", principal, persona CP1). Its sibling assertion **a_005** from the same record gives the birth as "Born at Trier, Rhine Province, Germany."
- **Tree person I1** (Patrick Flynn, male, birth ~1845, Ireland) is the only candidate. His parents are I2 (Thomas) and I3 (Mary).
- **Score:** `same_person` returned 0.85 for a_002 against I1. The score is recorded, but it does not authorize a link.
- **Nothing was written.** No `person_evidence` entry was created, and no facts were materialized. There are no conflicts or rejected links in the project, so the Ireland birthplace is not settled by any resolved conflict.

Next steps for the researcher:
- Decide whether the Trier baptism belongs to a different Patrick Flynn or whether the tree's Ireland birthplace is wrong. This is a conflict-resolution question.
- If you judge the record is not this person, say so and I can record a rejection.
- The record's date is not extracted, so I could not run a date check against I1's ~1845 birth. Extracting the date would help.

---
I could not tie the Trier, Germany baptism of Patrick Flynn to the Patrick Flynn in the tree, because the record gives his birthplace as Germany and the tree gives Ireland, and nothing in the project settles that disagreement. The name and the tree's other facts are consistent with him, so the record may still be about him, but I have left it unlinked and recorded no judgement. The next step is for you to decide whether the Trier baptism is this family's Patrick or a different man, and then I can either record that decision or check the record's date against the tree.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The person-evidence agent has completed the work. Here is its report:

---

**Linking src_001 (1875 SF Great Register) to Hermann Gaetjen (I1)**

The agent linked all nine assertions (a_001–a_009) from the 1875 San Francisco Great Register to **I1 Hermann Gaetjen** at **"probable" confidence** (identity score 0.43). No separate stub was created.

**Reasoning for the link:**
- Name varies only by spelling (Gatjen vs. Gaetjen), given name matches.
- Register's age of 21 gives a birth year of ~1854 — consistent with the 1871 index (b. 1854 Prussia), though 5 years off from the tree's unsourced "about 1859."
- German birthplace fits the index's "Prussia."
- No facts on the register contradict I1.

---

**Three open problems:**

1. **Birth year conflict.** I1 now has two birth-year facts (~1859 unsourced vs. ~1854 from the register). **Conflict-resolution is needed.**

2. **Naturalization interval.** The 1871 New York arrival → 1875 naturalization is only ~4 years 2 months, short of the required 5-year residency. The tree tool flagged a coherence contradiction. This caps the link at "probable."

3. **German origin still unnarrowed.** The register says only "Germany"; the index says "Prussia." The specific home place question remains open.

---

**Recommended next step:** Check the San Francisco naturalization court record (collection 2125028) for the court's own arrival and residence dates, then run conflict-resolution on the birth year.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
Linked all 20 assertions from the 1870 and 1880 Maury County records to the Weller family in the tree, but every link is capped at `probable` because nothing on file explains the move from Horsham, Sussex to Tennessee.

**Links written (11 in src_001, 11 in src_002; all score 0.78):**
- **William Weller (I1):** 1870 head (pe_001, pe_002, pe_011), 1880 head (pe_012, pe_013, pe_018). The 1880 wife and son relationship assertions also name him as head (pe_019, pe_022).
- **Mary Weller (I2):** 1870 (pe_003, pe_004), 1880 wife (pe_014, pe_015), and the wife relationship (pe_019 focus side).
- **James Weller (I3):** 1870 only (pe_005, pe_006). He is absent from 1880.
- **Ellen Weller (I4):** 1870 only (pe_007, pe_008). She is absent from 1880.
- **George Weller (I5):** 1870 (pe_009, pe_010) and 1880 son (pe_016, pe_017), plus the son relationship (pe_020 focus side).

Dates agree with the tree in every case (gap 0 years on each). Birthplace England fits Horsham. Names and household makeup match the 1861 Horsham listing.

**Why probable, not confident:** The tree's last residence for this family is Horsham in 1861. Maury County is 4,228 miles (6,804 km) away. The Tennessee FamilySearch wiki page has no sentence naming an arrival from England, and the project holds no passenger list, naturalization, or land record bridging the move. Under the policy, that caps every link in both records.

**Household check (1880):** James (about 28) and Ellen (about 25) have no recorded death before 1880. Their absence from the 1880 household is an open identity question. They may have married or left home, been enumerated elsewhere, or this may be a different family. This is not resolved by these links.

**Edges:** Census household record. The Couple and parent-child edges for this family already exist in the tree (sourced to the 1851 and 1861 Horsham censuses), so I did not add duplicates.

**Materialized:** Facts from both records were written onto I1 through I5 with source references. No vital-fact conflicts surfaced.

**Warnings:** `person_warnings` returned one "implausible" nonStandardPlace warning per tree person. The 1870 and 1880 Maury residence facts on I1 have no standard place, and the 1851 and 1861 Horsham facts on each person are also unlinked to standard places. No impossible-date warnings.

**Next:** The unexplained England-to-Tennessee move caps every link at probable, so the question should be settled by finding a passenger list, naturalization, or other record of the move. The James and Ellen absence from 1880 needs a separate search.

---

Linked William, Mary, and their children to the 1870 and 1880 Maury County, Tennessee census households. The match is "probably the same people" for every person. The names, ages, and English birthplaces all fit the 1861 Horsham household, but the family moved about 4,200 miles to Tennessee after 1861 and nothing on file explains that move, so I could not go higher. James and Ellen, who appear in 1870, are missing from 1880 with no recorded death, so it is unclear whether they left home, were counted elsewhere, or belong to a different family. Next, the family's move from England needs a passenger list, naturalization, or similar record, and James and Ellen's whereabouts in 1880 need to be traced.
